Dolge Orlick was working with us the next day when I reminded Joe that I had a half-day off. He didn't say anything right away because he and Joe were busy with a piece of hot metal, and I was working the bellows. But later, he leaned on his hammer and said, 'Hey, boss, you're not going to play favorites, are you? If Pip gets a half-day off, I should get one too.' I think he was about twenty-five, but he always talked about himself like he was an old man. Joe asked him, 'What would you do with a half-day off?' Orlick replied, 'What's Pip going to do with it? I can do the same things he can.' Joe said, 'Pip's going into town.' Orlick shot back, 'Well, I'm going into town too. Just because Pip can go doesn't mean I shouldn't be able to.' Joe told him not to get angry, but Orlick just grumbled, 'I'll get angry if I want to. Some people think they're so special just because they get to go into town.' The boss didn't want to deal with Orlick when he was in a bad mood, so Orlick went back to work, pulled out a red-hot bar, and pretended to stab me with it. He swung it around my head, put it on the anvil, and started hammering away, like he was pounding out his frustration. Finally, when he'd cooled down a bit, he said, 'Okay, boss, I'm ready to talk now.' Joe asked him if he was feeling better, and Orlick just grunted, 'Yeah, I'm fine.' Joe said, 'You usually do your job just like everyone else, so let's just give everyone the half-day off.' My sister had been standing outside, listening in without saying a word - she was always snooping around and eavesdropping. As soon as she heard the decision, she looked in through one of the windows.

He lived with a man who took care of a sluice out on the marshes. It was as if he was always thinking that it was strange he didn't have any thoughts. This man, a skilled worker, didn't like me. When I was little, he told me that the Devil lived in a dark corner of the blacksmith shop and that he knew the Devil well. “Biddy,” I said, after swearing her to secrecy, “I have a strong desire to become a gentleman.” “Oh, I wouldn’t, if I were you,” she replied. “I don’t think it would be the right choice.” “Biddy,” I said, with a hint of sternness, “I have specific reasons for wanting to be a gentleman.” “You know what’s best for you, Pip,” she said, “but don’t you think you’re happier as you are?” “Biddy,” I exclaimed, with growing impatience, “I am not happy at all as I am. I have never taken to my trade or my life since I was apprenticed. Don’t be ridiculous.” “Was I being ridiculous?” Biddy asked, quietly raising an eyebrow. “I apologize if I was; I didn’t mean to be. I only want what’s best for you, and for you to be content.” “Well, then, understand once and for all,” I said, “that I will never be content, or anything but miserable, unless I can lead a very different life from the one I lead now.” “That’s a shame,” Biddy said, shaking her head with a sorrowful expression. I had often thought the same, and in my internal struggle, I was half inclined to shed tears of frustration and distress when Biddy echoed my sentiment. I told her she was right, and I knew it was regrettable, but it was unavoidable. “If I could have settled into my life,” I said to Biddy, pulling at the short grass nearby, much like I used to pull my feelings out of my hair and kick them away, “if I could have been even half as fond of the forge as I was when I was little, I know it would have been much better for me. You, Joe, and I would have wanted for nothing, and Joe and I might have even become partners when I finished my apprenticeship. I might have even grown up to be worthy of your company, and we might have sat on this very bank on a fine Sunday, as very different people. I would have been good enough for you, wouldn’t I, Biddy?” Biddy sighed as she gazed out at the ships sailing by, and replied, “Yes, I’m not overly particular.” It didn’t sound like a compliment, but I knew she meant well. “Instead of that,” I said, pulling up more grass and chewing on a blade or two, “look at how I’m doing. I’m dissatisfied, uncomfortable, and—what would it matter to me, being coarse and common, if no one had pointed it out?” Biddy turned to face me, looking at me more intently than she had at the ships. “That wasn’t a very kind or truthful thing to say,” she remarked, directing her gaze back to the ships. “Who said it?” I was taken aback, as I had spoken without thinking. Mr. Jaggers said, “First, you should acquire some new clothes, not your work clothes. Let us say this day next week. You will need some money.” He pulled out a long purse with great composure, counted out twenty guineas on the table, and slid them over to me. This was the first time he had moved his leg from the chair. As he sat astride the chair, swinging his purse and eyeing Joe, he asked, “Well, Joseph Gargery, you seem astonished?” Joe replied, “I am!” in a very resolute manner. Mr. Jaggers reminded him, “It was understood that you wanted nothing for yourself, remember?” Joe confirmed, “It was understood, and it still is, and it always will be the same.” Mr. Jaggers swung his purse, saying, “But what if my instructions were to give you a gift as compensation?” Joe asked, “Compensation for what?” Mr. Jaggers replied, “For the loss of Pip's services.” Joe placed his hand on my shoulder with a gentle touch, like a woman's. I have often thought of him as a steam-hammer, capable of crushing a man or handling an eggshell with care, due to his combination of strength and gentleness. Joe said, “Pip is welcome to go freely with his services, to honour and fortune, as no words can express. But if you think money can compensate me for the loss of the little child who came to the forge and was my best friend...” Oh, dear good Joe, whom I was so ready to leave and so ungrateful to, I see you again with your muscular blacksmith's arm before your eyes, your broad chest heaving, and your voice fading away. Oh, dear good faithful tender Joe, I feel the loving tremble of your hand on my arm, as solemnly this day as if it had been the rustle of an angel's wing. I encouraged Joe at the time, lost in the complexities of my future fortunes, unable to retrace the paths we had walked together. I begged Joe to be comforted, reminding him that we had always been the best of friends and would continue to be so. Joe wiped his eyes with his wrist, as if trying to gouge himself, but said no more. Mr. Jaggers watched this exchange, seeming to view Joe as a simpleton and me as his caretaker. When it was over, he said, weighing the purse in his hand, “Now, Joseph Gargery, I warn you this is your last chance. No half-measures with me. If you mean to accept a gift that I have been instructed to give you, speak out, and you shall have it. If, on the other hand, you mean to say...” But to his great surprise, Joe suddenly turned on him, displaying every intention of engaging in a fierce fight.

And yet I couldn't,” said Mr. Pumblechook, rising from his seat once more, “look at One—and also toast One—without once more expressing—May I—_may_ I—?” I gave him permission, and he shook hands with me again, drained his glass, and turned it over. I did the same, and the wine went straight to my head, as if I had turned myself upside down before drinking. Mr. Pumblechook served me the liver wing and the best slice of tongue, taking little care of himself in comparison. “Ah, poultry, poultry! You never thought,” said Mr. Pumblechook, addressing the fowl on the platter, “when you were a young bird, what lay in store for you. You never imagined you would be a meal under this humble roof for someone like—Call it a weakness, if you will,” said Mr. Pumblechook, getting up again, “but may I? _may_ I—?” It was becoming unnecessary to repeat the form of saying he might, so he proceeded at once. I was amazed he didn't hurt himself with my knife, considering how often he did it. After eating for a while, he continued, “And your sister, who had the honour of raising you by hand! It's a sad picture to think that she's no longer capable of fully understanding the honour. May—” I saw he was about to ask again, and I stopped him. “We'll drink to her health,” I said. “Ah!” exclaimed Mr. Pumblechook, leaning back in his chair, completely relaxed in admiration, “that's how you know them, sir!” (I didn't know who Sir was, but it wasn't me, and there was no one else present); “that's how you know the noble-minded, sir! Ever forgiving and ever affable. To a common person, it might seem like repetition—but _may_ I—?” When he had finished, he sat down and drank to my sister's health. “Let us never be blind,” said Mr. Pumblechook, “to her temper flaws, but it's to be hoped she meant well.” Around this time, I started to notice that he was getting red in the face, while I felt my face was on fire from the wine. I told Mr. Pumblechook that I wanted my new clothes sent to his house, and he was overjoyed that I had chosen him. I explained that I wanted to avoid being seen in the village, and he praised my decision. He implied that he was the only one worthy of my trust, and—in short, might he? Then he asked me if I remembered our childhood games with numbers and how we had gone together to have me apprenticed, and, in effect, how he had always been my favourite friend and chosen companion? Even if I had drunk ten times as much wine as I had, I would have known that he had never been that close to me, and I would have rejected the idea in my heart. Yet, despite this, I felt convinced that I had misjudged him and that he was a sensible, practical, and kind person.

And yet I couldn't,” said Mr. Pumblechook, getting up again, “look at you and raise a glass without saying it again - may I, may I? I gave him the okay, and he shook my hand again, downed his drink, and turned his glass over. I did the same, and if I had flipped myself over before drinking, the wine couldn't have hit me harder. Mr. Pumblechook helped me to the best part of the liver and the top slice of tongue - none of the lower-quality cuts now - and didn't worry too much about his own serving. 'Oh, poultry, poultry!' Mr. Pumblechook exclaimed, talking to the food on his plate. 'You never thought, when you were young, what was in store for you. You had no idea you'd end up being served under this humble roof for someone like... Call it a weakness if you want,' said Mr. Pumblechook, getting up again, 'but may I, may I?' It was getting pointless to keep giving him permission, so he just went ahead. I have no idea how he managed to do it so many times without accidentally stabbing himself with my knife. 'And your sister,' he continued, after eating for a bit, 'who had the honor of raising you by hand. It's sad to think that she's not fully aware of the honor she's given you. May...' I saw him getting ready to ask again, so I cut him off. 'Let's drink to her health,' I said. 'Ah!' cried Mr. Pumblechook, leaning back in his chair, completely impressed. 'That's how you treat people with class, sir!' - though I have no idea who 'sir' was, since it wasn't me and there was no one else there. 'That's how you know someone with a noble mind, sir - always forgiving and always friendly. To a regular person, it might seem like I'm repeating myself, but... may I?' After he did it again, he sat back down and drank to my sister's health. 'Let's not ignore her flaws,' said Mr. Pumblechook, 'but hopefully, she meant well.' Around this time, I started to notice that Mr. Pumblechook's face was getting red, and as for me, I felt like my whole face was burning from the wine. I told Mr. Pumblechook that I wanted my new clothes sent to his house, and he was over the moon that I was giving him such an honor. I explained that I wanted to avoid drawing attention to myself in the village, and he thought it was a great idea. He implied that he was the only one worthy of my trust, and... well, might he? Then he asked me if I remembered the times we played with numbers as kids and how we went to get me set up as an apprentice, and basically, how he had always been my favorite person and closest friend. Even if I had ten times as much wine as I did, I would have known that he never actually felt that way about me, and deep down, I would have rejected the idea. Still, for some reason, I felt convinced that I had misjudged him and that he was actually a sensible, practical, and kind guy.

Mr. Pumblechook stood up again and said, 'I'd like to make a toast to someone special. May I?' I told him it was okay, and we shook hands. Then we drank our wine. I felt the wine go straight to my head. Mr. Pumblechook helped me get some food, giving me the best pieces. He didn't take much for himself. 'You didn't know what would happen to you when you were young,' he said to the food. 'You didn't know you'd be eaten here today.' He got up again and said, 'May I?' I noticed that Mr. Pumblechook's face was getting red, and I felt my face burning from the wine. I told him I wanted to send my new clothes to his house, and he was thrilled. I discovered that Wemmick was the clerk in the adjacent room. As he stepped out, another clerk was summoned from upstairs to take his place, and I accompanied him into the street after bidding farewell to my guardian. We encountered a new group of people lingering outside, but Wemmick effortlessly navigated through them by stating calmly yet firmly, 'I assure you, it's pointless; he won't engage with any of you,' and we soon cleared a path and continued on our way side by side.

As we walked, I took the opportunity to observe Mr. Wemmick in the daylight. I found him to be a somewhat austere man, slightly below average height, with a wooden face whose features seemed to have been roughly hewn with a blunt instrument. There were a few marks on his face that could have been dimples if the material had been more pliable and the tool more refined, but instead, they appeared as mere indentations. The instrument had attempted to create a few of these decorative touches above his nose but had abandoned the effort without smoothing them out. I surmised that he was a bachelor, given the worn state of his linen, and he seemed to have experienced numerous losses, as evidenced by the multiple mourning rings he wore, in addition to a brooch depicting a lady and a weeping willow beside a tomb with an urn. I also noticed that several rings and seals hung from his watch-chain, as if he were heavily burdened with memories of departed friends. His eyes sparkled - small, sharp, and black - and his lips were thin, wide, and mottled. To the best of my knowledge, he had possessed these features for forty to fifty years.

'Had you never been to London before?' Mr. Wemmick inquired of me.

'No,' I replied.

'I, too, was once new to this city,' said Mr. Wemmick. 'It's strange to think about now.'

'Are you well acquainted with London now?' I asked.

'Oh, yes,' said Mr. Wemmick. 'I'm familiar with its ways.'

'Is it a particularly wicked place?' I asked, more out of a desire to make conversation than to gain insight.

'You can be deceived, robbed, or murdered in London,' he said. 'However, there are plenty of people elsewhere who would do the same to you.'

'If there's ill will between you and them,' I added, attempting to soften the statement.

'Oh, I don't know about ill will,' Mr. Wemmick responded. 'There isn't much of that about. They'll do it if there's something to be gained.'

'That makes it worse,' I said.

'Do you think so?' Mr. Wemmick replied. 'I'd say it's much the same.'

He wore his hat at the back of his head and gazed straight ahead, walking with a self-assured air as if nothing in the streets warranted his attention. His mouth seemed to be perpetually frozen in a mechanical smile, giving him a somewhat artificial appearance. We had reached the top of Holborn Hill before I realized that this was merely a facade, and he wasn't actually smiling at all.

'Do you know where Mr. Matthew Pocket resides?' I asked Mr. Wemmick.

'Yes,' he replied, nodding in a particular direction. 'He lives in Hammersmith, to the west of London.'

'Is that far?'

The gusts had been so intense that they had stripped the lead from the roofs of tall buildings in town, and in the countryside, trees had been uprooted and windmill sails had been carried away. Reports from the coast had been grim, with accounts of shipwrecks and loss of life. The day that had just ended had been the most severe, with violent blasts of rain accompanying the fierce winds. As I sat down to read, the alterations that had been made to the Temple since then were not yet in place, and it still had a somewhat isolated character, exposed as it was to the river. Our home was at the top of the last house, and the wind rushing up the river that night shook the house violently, much like the sound of cannon fire or the crashing of waves. When the rain lashed against the windows, I felt as though I might have imagined myself in a storm-battered lighthouse, the windows rocking back and forth. Occasionally, the smoke would billow down the chimney, as if it too were reluctant to venture out into the tempestuous night. When I opened the doors and peered down the staircase, I found that the lamps had been extinguished by the wind, and when I cautiously approached the windows, shielding my face with my hands, I saw that the lamps in the courtyard and on the bridges and shore were also being buffeted by the gale, while the coal fires on the barges were being swept away like glowing embers in the rain. I had placed my watch on the table, intending to stop reading at eleven o'clock. As I closed my book, the sound of Saint Paul's and the numerous church clocks in the City striking the hour filled the air, though the wind distorted the sound. I was lost in thought, pondering the way the wind was assaulting the clocks, when I heard the sound of footsteps on the stairs. With this goal in mind, I must secure a list of at least five hundred subscribers before launching the magazine; I have already gathered nearly two hundred. Although these letters are brief and hastily written, they demonstrate the presence of qualities often denied to Mr. Poe, such as humility, perseverance, and a capacity for genuine and grateful friendship. These traits were undoubtedly characteristic of him when he was sane, and they have consistently been our experience of him throughout our five- or six-year friendship. It is easier to believe what we have personally witnessed than what we have only heard, and so we remember him with admiration and respect; the descriptions of him during periods of moral insanity seem to us like portraits of a man we have only known in health, painted during times of sickness. It was a difficult fate that she was struggling to overcome, as Mr. Poe's writing, though meticulous and refined, was not well-suited to the popular taste and therefore not well-rewarded.

He became so focused on the details that he lost sight of the bigger picture. This, Dupin argued, was a common error - being too intense in one's pursuit of knowledge. Truth, he claimed, is often superficial, and the most important knowledge can be found in the broader landscape, rather than in the depths of intense scrutiny. To illustrate this point, Dupin used the example of observing the stars. By glancing at a star indirectly, one can see it more clearly than by staring directly at it. This, he suggested, is because the peripheral vision is more sensitive to faint light. Similarly, in investigation, a more refined and nuanced approach can be more effective than a direct and intense one. Dupin proposed that they conduct their own investigation into the murders, rather than relying on the official inquiry. He suggested that this would not only provide amusement but also allow them to form their own opinion. As he had a personal connection with the Prefect of Police, G——, he was able to obtain the necessary permission to visit the crime scene. They made their way to the Rue Morgue, a dismal street located between the Rue Richelieu and the Rue St. Roch. It was late in the afternoon when they arrived, and the house was easy to find due to the crowd of onlookers gathered across the street, staring at the closed shutters with a mixture of curiosity and morbid fascination.

I had to agree with the rest of Paris that the murders were a complete enigma. I couldn't see any way to track down the killer. 'We shouldn't judge the investigation based on what we've seen so far,' Dupin said. 'The Paris police, who are often praised for their sharp instincts, are clever but that's about it. They don't have a systematic approach, just a lot of flashy tactics that often don't achieve their goals. They make a big show of their efforts, but these efforts are often poorly planned and remind me of someone trying to listen to music more clearly by putting on a robe. Sometimes they get surprising results, but most of the time it's just because they're diligent and active. When that's not enough, their plans fall apart. Vidocq, for example, was good at making educated guesses and persisted in his investigations, but he didn't have a thoughtful approach and often made mistakes because he was too focused on the details. He was so close to the object of his investigation that he lost sight of the bigger picture. There's such a thing as being too obsessed with finding the truth. Truth isn't always hidden; in fact, when it comes to the most important things, I think it's usually right on the surface. The problem is that we often look for it in the wrong places. This kind of mistake is similar to what happens when we try to study the stars. If we glance at a star out of the corner of our eye, we can see it clearly, but if we stare directly at it, it becomes dimmer. This is because our eyes are more sensitive to light when we're not looking directly at something. By being too intense in our pursuit of knowledge, we can actually confuse and weaken our thinking. It's possible to make even the brightest star disappear by staring at it too long. 'As for these murders, let's do some investigating of our own before we form an opinion. It'll be an interesting challenge,' Dupin said. I thought it was an odd way to describe it, but I didn't say anything. 'Besides, Le Bon once did me a favor, and I'm grateful. We'll go check out the scene and see what we can find. I know the Police Prefect, G——, and I'm sure he'll let us take a look.' We got the necessary permission and headed to the Rue Morgue. The street is one of those run-down alleys between the Rue Richelieu and the Rue St. Roch. We arrived late in the afternoon, since it's a long way from where we live. The house was easy to find, since there were still a lot of people standing across the street, staring up at the closed shutters out of curiosity.

I agreed with the people of Paris that the murders were a mystery that couldn't be solved. I didn't see how it would be possible to find the killer. Dupin said, 'We shouldn't judge the investigation by what we see on the surface. The Paris police are clever, but they don't have a systematic approach. They make a big show of their efforts, but often these efforts are not well thought out and don't achieve their goals. Sometimes they get surprising results, but this is usually due to their hard work and activity rather than any clever strategy. When these qualities aren't enough, their plans fail. For example, Vidocq was a good guesser and a persistent man, but he often made mistakes because he focused too much on the details and lost sight of the bigger picture. He was so focused on one thing that he missed the overall truth. This shows that it's possible to be too thorough in an investigation. The truth is not always hidden, but rather it's often right in front of us. I think that the most important knowledge is often the most obvious. The problem is that we often look too hard for the truth and end up missing it. This is like trying to look at a star directly - if you look at it straight on, it can be hard to see, but if you look at it out of the corner of your eye, you can see it more clearly. If we think too much about something, we can confuse ourselves and make it harder to understand. Let's look into the murders ourselves before we decide what to think about them. It will be an interesting challenge, and I also want to help Le Bon, who once did me a favor. We can go to the scene of the crime and see it for ourselves. I know the Prefect of Police, and I can get us permission to visit the house. We got the permission and went to the Rue Morgue, which is a poor street between the Rue Richelieu and the Rue St. Roch. It was late in the afternoon when we arrived, and there were still many people standing outside the house, looking up at the closed shutters with curiosity.

The scent had remained constant, with no break in the chain of events. I had followed the secret to its final conclusion, which was the nail. It appeared identical to the one in the other window, but this similarity was essentially meaningless when considering that the trail ended here. 'There must be something wrong with the nail,' I thought. Upon touching it, the head and about a quarter of an inch of the shank came off in my hand. The rest of the shank was lodged in the gimlet-hole, where it had been broken off. The break was old, with rust covering the edges, and seemed to have been caused by a hammer blow that had partially embedded the head of the nail in the bottom sash. I carefully replaced the head portion in its original position, and the nail appeared whole again - the crack was no longer visible. When I pressed the spring and raised the sash a few inches, the head moved with it, remaining securely in place. After closing the window, the nail seemed perfect once more. The mystery, up to this point, was now solved. The killer had escaped through the window that overlooked the bed. As they left, the window had closed, either on its own or intentionally, and the spring had fastened it, leading the police to mistakenly believe the nail was holding it in place. The next question was how the killer had descended. During our walk around the building, I had already formed an opinion on this matter. About five and a half feet from the window in question, a lightning rod was installed. It would have been impossible for anyone to reach the window from this rod, let alone enter it. However, I noticed that the shutters on the fourth story were of a particular type known as ferrades, which are rarely used today but often found on old mansions in Lyons and Bordeaux. These shutters resemble a regular door, except the lower half is latticed, providing a good grip for the hands. In this case, the shutters were over three and a half feet wide. When we saw them from the back of the house, they were both half open, standing at right angles to the wall. It's likely that the police, like myself, examined the back of the building, but when looking at the ferrades from the side, they may not have noticed their width or failed to consider it properly. As a result, they probably gave this area only a cursory examination, having already convinced themselves that no one could have escaped this way.

The scent had never been lost for even a moment. There was no flaw in any link of the chain. I had traced the secret to its ultimate result, and that result was the nail. It had, I say, in every respect, the appearance of its fellow in the other window, but this fact was essentially meaningless when compared with the consideration that here, at this point, the trail ended. 'There must be something wrong about the nail,' I said. I touched it, and the head, with about a quarter of an inch of the shank, came off in my fingers. The rest of the shank was in the gimlet-hole where it had been broken off. The fracture was an old one, as its edges were covered in rust, and had apparently been caused by the blow of a hammer, which had partially embedded the head portion of the nail in the top of the bottom sash. I now carefully replaced this head portion in the indentation whence I had taken it, and the resemblance to a perfect nail was complete - the fissure was invisible. Pressing the spring, I gently raised the sash for a few inches; the head went up with it, remaining firm in its bed. I closed the window, and the appearance of the whole nail was again perfect. The mystery, so far, was now solved. The assassin had escaped through the window that looked upon the bed. Dropping of its own accord upon his exit, or perhaps purposely closed, it had become fastened by the spring; and it was the retention of this spring that had been mistaken by the police for that of the nail, making further inquiry seem unnecessary. The next question is that of the mode of descent. Upon this point, I had been satisfied during my walk with you around the building. About five and a half feet from the casement in question, there runs a lightning rod. From this rod, it would have been impossible for anyone to reach the window itself, let alone enter it. I observed, however, that the shutters of the fourth story were of a peculiar kind called ferrades by Parisian carpenters - a kind rarely used today, but often seen on very old mansions in Lyons and Bordeaux. They are in the form of an ordinary door, except that the lower half is latticed or worked in open trellis, thus providing an excellent hold for the hands. In the present instance, these shutters are fully three and a half feet broad. When we saw them from the rear of the house, they were both about half open - that is to say, they stood off at right angles from the wall. It is likely that the police, as well as myself, examined the back of the tenement, but if so, in looking at these ferrades in the line of their breadth, they did not notice this great breadth itself, or at all events, failed to take it into due consideration. In fact, having once satisfied themselves that no escape could have been made in this quarter, they would naturally give it a very cursory examination.

The scent had never been lost for a moment. I had followed the secret to its final result, which was a nail. It looked like the other nails in the window, but that didn't matter. What mattered was that this was the end of the trail. I thought, 'There must be something wrong with this nail.' I touched it, and the head came off in my fingers. The rest of the nail was broken off in the hole where it had been. The break was old and had been made by a hammer. I put the head back where it belonged, and the nail looked perfect again. When I opened the window a little, the head stayed in place. I closed the window, and the nail looked whole again. The mystery was starting to make sense. The killer had escaped through the window by the bed. When they left, the window closed by itself or was closed on purpose, and it got stuck because of the spring. The police thought the nail was holding the window shut, so they didn't look any further. The next question was how the killer got down. When we walked around the building, I figured it out. There was a lightning rod about five and a half feet away from the window, but it was too far to reach. I noticed that the shutters on the fourth floor were a special kind called ferrades. They have a lattice bottom and are wide enough to grab onto. When we saw them from the back, they were half open. The police probably looked at them from the side and didn't notice how wide they were, or they didn't think it was important. They probably didn't look closely because they thought no one could have escaped that way.

We assure you, we mean no harm to you. As a gentleman and a Frenchman, I give you my word that we do not intend to cause you any injury. I am well aware that you are not responsible for the atrocities committed in the Rue Morgue. However, it would be unwise to deny that you are somehow involved in the events that transpired. From my previous statements, you must have gathered that I have had access to information about this matter, information that you could not have possibly imagined. The situation stands as follows: you have not done anything that you could have avoided doing, and certainly nothing that would render you guilty. You did not even take advantage of the opportunity to rob when you could have done so with impunity. You have nothing to hide and no reason to conceal anything. On the other hand, every principle of honor obliges you to reveal all that you know. An innocent man is currently imprisoned, accused of the crime for which you can identify the true perpetrator. The sailor had largely regained his composure by the time Dupin finished speaking, but his initial bold demeanor had vanished. 'So help me God!' he exclaimed after a brief pause, 'I will tell you everything I know about this affair, but I do not expect you to believe half of what I say - I would be a fool to think otherwise. Nevertheless, I am innocent, and I will confess everything, even if it costs me my life.' What he recounted was, in essence, the following: he had recently returned from a voyage to the Indian Archipelago. During an excursion into the interior of Borneo, he and a companion had captured an Ourang-Outang. After his companion's death, the animal became his sole responsibility. Following significant difficulties caused by the animal's ferocity during the return voyage, he eventually managed to safely house it at his Parisian residence. To avoid drawing unwanted attention from his neighbors, he kept the animal secluded until it recovered from a foot injury sustained on board ship. His ultimate intention was to sell the animal. Upon returning home from a night of revelry with fellow sailors, he found the beast in his bedroom, having broken free from a closet where it was supposed to be securely confined. The animal was sitting in front of a mirror, attempting to shave itself with a razor, having apparently observed its master doing so through the keyhole. Terrified by the sight of such a dangerous weapon in the possession of a ferocious animal, the man was initially at a loss for what to do. However, he had grown accustomed to calming the creature with a whip, and he now resorted to this method. Upon seeing the whip, the Ourang-Outang immediately sprang through the door, down the stairs, and out a window that happened to be open, into the street. The Frenchman followed in desperation, with the ape occasionally stopping to look back and gesture at its pursuer, until the Frenchman had almost caught up with it.

In the official announcement of the reward, it was stated that any accomplice who came forward to testify against their fellow culprits would be granted a full pardon. Additionally, a private notice from a committee of citizens was appended to the announcement, offering a further 10,000 francs on top of the amount proposed by the authorities. As a result, the total reward stood at a minimum of 30,000 francs, a sum that seemed extraordinary considering the humble circumstances of the victim and the frequency of such heinous crimes in large cities. It was widely believed that the mystery of the murder would soon be solved. However, despite a few arrests that initially seemed promising, nothing was uncovered that could implicate the suspected parties, and they were released immediately. It is surprising that nearly three weeks had passed since the discovery of the body, and yet no progress had been made in shedding light on the subject, before Dupin and I even heard a whisper of the events that had caused such public outcry. We had been so engrossed in our research that it had been almost a month since either of us had ventured out, received a visitor, or glanced at the major news articles in the daily papers. The first news of the murder reached us through G——, who visited us in person. He arrived early in the afternoon of July 13, 18—, and stayed with us until late at night. He was frustrated by his failure to track down the assassins, and his reputation, he claimed, was on the line. His honor, he said, was also at stake, and the public's eyes were upon him. He was willing to make any sacrifice to unravel the mystery. He ended his somewhat amusing speech with a compliment to Dupin's exceptional abilities and made him a direct and generous proposal, the details of which I am not at liberty to disclose, but which had no bearing on the main subject of my account. Dupin politely deflected the compliment but accepted the proposal without hesitation, despite its provisional nature. Once this was settled, the Prefect launched into a detailed explanation of his own theories, interspersing them with lengthy comments on the evidence, which we had not yet seen. He spoke at length, and undoubtedly with great learning, while I ventured the occasional suggestion as the night wore on. Dupin, seated in his usual armchair, was the epitome of attentive listening, wearing spectacles throughout the interview. An occasional glance beneath the green glasses was enough to convince me that he was sleeping soundly, albeit silently, during the seven or eight hours that preceded the Prefect's departure. The next morning, I obtained a comprehensive report of all the evidence gathered from the Prefecture and collected copies of every newspaper article that had published decisive information about the case, from start to finish.

No one crossed the threshold to discuss the matter in the Rue Pavée St. Andrée, not even with those residing in the same building. M. St. Eustache, Marie's lover and intended husband, who lived with her mother, claimed he was unaware of the discovery of his intended's body until the following morning. It was then that M. Beauvais entered his room and informed him of the news. The reception of this news seemed surprisingly subdued, given its significance. The journal attempted to convey the impression that Marie's relatives were apathetic about her disappearance, which would be inconsistent with the idea that they believed the recovered body to be hers. The journal's insinuations suggested that Marie had left the city with the knowledge of her friends, due to a scandal involving her reputation, and that upon finding a similar-looking corpse, her friends took the opportunity to deceive the public into believing she was dead. However, L'Etoile was too hasty in its accusations. It was proven that the supposed apathy did not exist; the elderly lady was extremely frail and agitated, unable to attend to her duties. St. Eustache, far from being calm, was overcome with grief and behaved frantically, prompting M. Beauvais to ask a friend to take charge of him and prevent him from attending the disinterment examination. Furthermore, despite L'Etoile's claims that the corpse was reburied at public expense, that the family declined a private burial offer, and that no family member attended the ceremony, all these assertions were disproven. In a later issue, the paper attempted to cast suspicion on Beauvais himself. The editor stated that on one occasion, while Madame B—— was visiting Madame Rogêt, M. Beauvais, upon leaving, instructed her not to speak to the expected gendarme until he returned. It seemed that M. Beauvais had taken control of the entire matter, and for some reason, he was determined to be the only one involved in the proceedings, even going so far as to push the male relatives aside in a peculiar manner. He appeared to be strongly opposed to allowing the relatives to see the body. A circumstance that lent some credibility to the suspicion against Beauvais was the discovery, by a visitor to his office a few days before Marie's disappearance, of a rose in the keyhole and the name 'Marie' written on a nearby slate, while Beauvais was absent.

Beauvais because a visitor to his office had seen a rose in the keyhole of his door and the name 'Marie' written on a slate a few days before she disappeared.

To me, this article seems to reveal more about the enthusiasm of its writer than anything else. We must remember that newspapers often prioritize creating a stir and making a point over pursuing the truth. The truth is only sought when it aligns with the goal of creating a sensation. An article that simply echoes common opinion, no matter how well-founded, does not impress the masses. The general public tends to regard as insightful only those who propose provocative contradictions to the prevailing idea. In reasoning, just as in literature, it is the clever phrase that is most immediately and widely appreciated, even if it is of relatively low merit. What I am saying is that it is the combination of clever phrasing and dramatic flair in the idea that Marie Rogêt is still alive, rather than any genuine plausibility, that has led L'Etoile to propose it and made it appealing to the public. It's hard to tell which one will win in the end. But you're going to be okay. You'll have a lot of trouble and a lot of joy in your life. Sometimes you'll get hurt, and sometimes you'll get sick, but you'll always get better. There are two women who will be important in your life. One is rich, and the other is poor. You'll marry the poor one first, and then the rich one later. You should try to stay away from water as much as you can and not take any risks, because it's predicted that you'll get in trouble.

When I lit my candle and went to my room that night, my dad was sitting there. I had closed the door, and then I turned around and saw him. I used to be scared of him all the time because he would spank me so much. I thought I was scared of him now, but after a minute, I realized I wasn't. He was about fifty years old and looked it. His hair was long, tangled, and greasy, and it hung down in his face. You could see his eyes shining through his hair, which was all black with no gray. His face was white, but not a healthy white - it was a sickly color. His clothes were just rags. He had one foot resting on the other knee, and his boot was broken, with two of his toes sticking out. He would wiggle them every now and then. His hat was on the floor, an old black hat with the top caved in.

I stood there looking at him, and he looked at me with his chair tilted back a little. I put the candle down and noticed that the window was open, so he must have climbed in through the shed. He kept looking me up and down. After a while, he said, 'You're dressing pretty fancy, aren't you? You think you're a big deal, don't you?' 'Maybe I am, maybe I'm not,' I said. 'Don't talk back to me,' he said. 'You've gotten pretty full of yourself since I've been away. I'll take you down a peg before I'm done with you. You're educated, they say - you can read and write. You think you're better than your dad just because he can't, don't you?'

I figured someone would be hiding in the canoe, trying to trick people, and when they'd paddled out to it, they'd jump up and laugh. But that wasn't the case this time. It was a genuine drift-canoe, and I climbed in and paddled it to shore. I thought to myself, the old man will be pleased when he sees this - it's worth about ten dollars. However, when I got to shore, pap wasn't around, and as I was pulling the canoe into a small creek lined with vines and willows, I had another idea: I decided to hide it well, and instead of heading into the woods when I ran away, I'd travel down the river about fifty miles and set up camp in one spot, avoiding the hardship of walking on foot. The creek was close to our shanty, and I kept thinking I heard the old man approaching, but I managed to hide the canoe. Then I went to check around a cluster of willows, and there was the old man down the path, taking aim at a bird with his gun. So, he hadn't seen anything. When he came along, I was busy pulling in a trot line. He scolded me for being slow, but I told him I fell into the river, which explained why I was late. I knew he'd notice I was wet and start asking questions. We caught five catfish and headed home. After breakfast, we took a break to rest, as we were both exhausted. I started thinking that if I could come up with a way to keep pap and the widow from chasing after me, it would be more reliable than relying on luck to get far enough away before they noticed I was gone. Many things could go wrong. For a while, I didn't see a solution, but then pap got up to drink some water and said, 'Next time someone's snooping around here, you wake me up, you hear? That man wasn't here for any good. I would've shot him. Next time, you wake me up, you hear?' Then he lay back down and fell asleep again. But what he said gave me the idea I needed. I thought to myself, now I can make sure no one will think of following me. Around noon, we set out and walked along the bank. The river was rising quickly, and a lot of driftwood was floating by. Soon, part of a log raft came along - nine logs tied together. We took the skiff out and towed it to shore. Then we had dinner. Any reasonable person would have waited out the day to catch more driftwood, but that wasn't pap's way. Nine logs were enough for him; he had to hurry to town and sell them right away. So, he locked me in, took the skiff, and started off with the raft around half-past three. I figured he wouldn't be back that night.

Then it hit me - I figured the widow or the parson must have prayed for this bread to find me, and now it has. So I'm convinced there's something to that praying business, at least when someone like the widow or the parson does it. It just doesn't seem to work for me, and I reckon it only works for certain folks. I lit my pipe and took a long drag, continuing to watch the river. The ferry-boat was drifting with the current, and I thought I'd get a chance to see who was on board when it floated by, since it would come close to the shore where I found the bread. As it approached, I put out my pipe and snuck down to where I'd found the bread, hiding behind a log on the bank. I could peek through the fork in the log and see everything. Before long, the ferry-boat came along, drifting so close that someone could have walked ashore on a plank. Just about everybody in town was on that boat - Pap, Judge Thatcher, Bessie Thatcher, Jo Harper, Tom Sawyer, his Aunt Polly, Sid, Mary, and a whole lot more. Everyone was talking about the murder, but the captain interrupted, saying, 'Keep a sharp eye out, the current runs strongest here, and maybe the body has washed up and gotten tangled in the brush along the water's edge. I hope that's the case, anyway.' I wasn't hoping for that at all. They all crowded up to the rail, right in front of me, and fell silent, watching intently. I could see them plain as day, but they couldn't see me. Then the captain yelled, 'Stand back!' and the cannon fired off a blast that was so loud it left me deaf and blinded by the smoke. The boat floated on and disappeared around the bend of the island. When they got to the head of the island, they stopped firing and headed to the Missouri shore, then went back to town. I knew I was safe now - nobody else would be coming after me. I pulled my gear out of the canoe and set up a nice camp in the thick woods. I made a little tent out of my blankets to keep my stuff dry, and I caught a catfish and split it open with my saw. I thought I could land almost anywhere, but it wasn't that easy - the bank was too steep. I was nearly at the foot of the island before I found a suitable spot. I decided to head into the woods, figuring it was pointless to mess with rafts as long as they were moving the lantern around. I had my pipe, some dog-leg tobacco, and matches in my cap, which weren't wet, so I was all set.

And you haven't had any meat or bread to eat this whole time? Why didn't you catch some mud-turkles?

How were you supposed to catch them? You can't sneak up on them and grab them, and it's not like you can hit them with a rock. It's not like you could even try in the daytime without being seen.

That's true, you've had to stay in the woods the whole time. Did you hear them shooting the cannon?

Oh, yes. I knew they were after you. I saw them go by, watching them through the bushes.

Some young birds flew by, going a yard or two at a time and then landing. Jim said it was a sign that it was going to rain. He claimed that when young chickens flew like that, it meant rain, and he figured it was the same with young birds. I was going to catch some, but Jim wouldn't let me. He said it was bad luck. He told me that his father had been very sick once, and someone caught a bird, and his old grandmother said his father would die - and he did.

Jim also said you shouldn't count the things you're going to cook for dinner, or it would bring bad luck. And if you shook the tablecloth after sundown, that was bad luck too. He said that if a man owned a beehive and died, the bees had to be told about it before sunrise the next morning, or they would all get weak and stop working and die. Jim said bees wouldn't sting idiots, but I didn't believe him - I'd tried it before, and they didn't sting me.

I'd heard some of these things before, but not all of them. Jim knew all sorts of signs and superstitions. He claimed he knew almost everything. I pointed out that all the signs seemed to be about bad luck, so I asked him if there weren't any good-luck signs. He said:

There are hardly any, and they're not much use to you anyway. What's the point of knowing when good luck is coming? Do you want to try to avoid it? Every night, around ten o'clock, I'd sneak ashore in some small village and buy a little food, like meal or bacon, for ten or fifteen cents; sometimes I'd even snatch a chicken that wasn't roosting too comfortably and take it with me. Pap always said that if you get the chance to take a chicken, you should, because even if you don't want it yourself, you can always find someone who does, and a good deed is never forgotten. Although I never saw Pap turn down a chicken himself, that's what he always said, anyway.

In the mornings, before daylight, I'd slip into cornfields and take a watermelon, or a mushmelon, or a pumpkin, or some fresh corn. Pap claimed it wasn't wrong to borrow things as long as you planned to pay them back someday, but the widow said that was just a nice way of saying stealing, and no respectable person would do it. Jim thought the widow was partly right and Pap was partly right, so he suggested we pick a few things from the list and decide not to borrow them anymore, and that way it wouldn't be wrong to borrow the rest. We spent one whole night discussing it, drifting down the river, trying to decide whether to give up watermelons, cantaloupes, or mushmelons. By dawn, we'd made up our minds and decided to stop taking crabapples and persimmons. We felt better after that, and I was glad we'd made that decision, since crabapples are never any good, and persimmons wouldn't be ripe for a couple of months yet.

Now and then, we'd shoot a bird that got up too early or stayed up too late. All in all, we were living pretty well.

I asked Jim, “Am I, or am I not? You tell me this: Didn’t you take out the line in the canoe to tie up to the tow-head?” Jim replied, “No, I didn’t. What tow-head are you talking about? I haven’t seen any tow-head.” I pressed him, “You haven’t seen any tow-head? Look, didn’t the line come loose and the raft drift down the river, leaving you and the canoe behind in the fog?” Jim seemed puzzled, “What fog are you talking about?” I clarified, “The fog that’s been around all night. Didn’t we shout, and didn’t you shout, until we got mixed up in the islands and one of us got lost, and the other was just as good as lost because he didn’t know where he was? And didn’t I crash into a lot of those islands and have a terrible time, almost getting drowned? Isn’t that what happened, Jim? Tell me.” Jim responded, “This is all too much for me, Huck. I haven’t seen any fog, or islands, or troubles. I’ve been sitting here talking with you all night until you fell asleep about ten minutes ago, and I think I did the same. You couldn’t have gotten drunk in that time, so you must have been dreaming.” Jim was skeptical, “How could I have dreamed all that in just ten minutes?” I insisted, “You must have dreamed it, because none of it actually happened.” Jim thought for a moment, “But, Huck, it all seems so clear to me...” I interrupted, “It doesn’t matter how clear it seems; it’s just not true. I know, because I’ve been here the whole time.” Jim was quiet for about five minutes, thinking it over. Then he said, “Well, I reckon I did dream it, Huck; but I swear, it’s the most powerful dream I’ve ever had. And I’ve never had a dream before that’s left me feeling so tired.” I reassured him, “Well, that’s okay, because sometimes a dream can exhaust you just like anything else. But this one was a really vivid dream; tell me all about it, Jim.” So Jim started telling me the whole story, just as it had happened in his dream, although he embellished it quite a bit. He said the first tow-head represented a man who would try to help us, but the current symbolized another man who would try to take us away from him. Usually, boats going upstream don't come close to us, but on nights like this, they go right up the middle of the river. We could hear the boat coming, but we didn't see it well until it was close. It was heading straight for us. Sometimes boats do this to see how close they can get without hitting us. This boat was big and moving fast, with rows of lights that looked like glowworms. But then it suddenly appeared even bigger, with its furnace doors open and its front sticking out over us. Someone yelled at us, and the boat's bells rang to stop the engines. There was a lot of cursing and whistling, and Jim jumped into the water on one side while I jumped on the other. The boat smashed right through the raft. I dove down, trying to find the bottom of the river, because the boat's big wheel had to pass over me. I can hold my breath for a minute, but this time I stayed under for a minute and a half. Then I quickly swam back up to the surface, almost out of breath. I popped out of the water up to my armpits, blew out the water, and took a few deep breaths. The current was strong, and the boat started moving again just ten seconds after it stopped. I called out for Jim about a dozen times, but he didn't answer. So I grabbed a plank that was floating near me and started swimming towards the shore, pushing the plank in front of me. But then I realized the current was taking me to the left side of the river, so I changed direction and went that way.

There was a picture of a young woman standing at a window, gazing up at the moon with tears streaming down her face. She was holding an open letter with a black seal and clutching a locket to her mouth. The picture was captioned 'And Art Thou Gone Yes Thou Art Gone Alas.' I thought these pictures were nice, but they always gave me the shivers when I was feeling down. Everyone was sad that the artist had passed away, as she had planned to create many more works like these. You could see from what she had already done what a great loss it was. I figured that, given her temperament, she was probably happier in the graveyard. She was working on what was supposed to be her masterpiece when she fell ill, and she prayed every day and night to be allowed to live long enough to finish it. The picture showed a young woman in a long white dress, standing on the edge of a bridge, ready to jump, with her hair flowing down her back and tears running down her face. She had multiple arms folded across her chest, stretched out in front of her, and reaching up towards the moon - the idea was to decide which set of arms looked best and then erase the rest. However, she died before making up her mind, and now the picture hung over her bed, adorned with flowers on her birthday and hidden behind a curtain at other times. The woman in the picture had a sweet face, but all those arms made her look a bit too strange to me. This young artist used to keep a scrapbook, where she would paste obituaries, accidents, and stories of suffering from the Presbyterian Observer, and then write her own poetry about them. Her poetry was really good. For example, she wrote a poem about a boy named Stephen Dowling Bots who fell down a well and drowned. The poem went like this: ODE TO STEPHEN DOWLING BOTS, DEC’D. It asked if young Stephen had fallen ill and died, and if the people around him were sad and crying. But that wasn't what happened to Stephen Dowling Bots. He didn't die from whooping cough or measles, and he wasn't struck down by unrequited love or stomach troubles. No, his fate was different. He fell down a well, and by the time they pulled him out, it was too late. His spirit had already left this world and gone to a better place.

The following Sunday, we all attended church, which was about three miles away, with everyone riding horseback. The men brought their guns along, just like Buck did, and kept them between their knees or leaned them against the wall. The Shepherdsons did the same thing. The sermon was quite unpleasant, focusing on brotherly love and similar topics that seemed tedious, but everyone praised it as a good sermon. On the way home, they all discussed it, talking about faith, good deeds, and predestination, among other things, which made it seem like one of the most unpleasant Sundays I had experienced.

About an hour after dinner, everyone was dozing off, either in their chairs or in their rooms, and the atmosphere became quite dull. Buck and a dog were lying on the grass in the sun, fast asleep. I went up to my room, thinking I would take a nap as well. As I passed by, I saw Miss Sophia standing in her doorway, which was next to ours. She invited me into her room, closed the door softly, and asked if I liked her. I replied that I did, and then she asked if I would do something for her without telling anyone. I agreed, and she told me she had left her Testament at church, between two other books, and asked if I could sneak out and retrieve it for her without saying anything to anyone. I agreed to do so.

I slipped out and made my way to the church, where I found no one except maybe a few hogs, as there was no lock on the door and hogs like to stay on the puncheon floor during summer because it's cool. It's interesting to note that most people only attend church when they have to, but hogs are different. As I thought to myself, something seemed unusual; it wasn't normal for a girl to be so worried about a Testament. So, I shook it, and a small piece of paper fell out with '_Half-past two_' written on it in pencil. I searched the Testament but couldn't find anything else. The paper didn't make sense to me, so I put it back in the book and headed home.

When I got upstairs, Miss Sophia was waiting for me in her doorway. She pulled me into her room, closed the door, and then looked in the Testament until she found the paper. As soon as she read it, she looked happy, and before I could react, she grabbed me and gave me a squeeze, saying I was the best boy in the world and telling me not to tell anyone. Her face turned red, and her eyes sparkled, making her look very pretty. I was quite surprised, but once I caught my breath, I asked her what the paper meant. She asked if I had read it, and I said no. Then she asked if I could read writing, and I told her I could only read coarse handwriting. She said the paper was just a bookmark to keep her place, and I could go play now.

Jim claimed it was spirits, but I disagreed, saying spirits wouldn't use phrases like 'Dern the dern fog.' As soon as night fell, we set off, and when we reached the middle of the river, we let the current take us wherever it wanted. We'd light our pipes, dangle our legs in the water, and talk about various things. We usually went naked, both day and night, as long as the mosquitoes allowed it. The new clothes Buck's family made for me were too nice to be comfortable, and besides, I wasn't too fond of clothes anyway. Sometimes we'd have the entire river to ourselves for a long time. Over yonder, we'd see the banks and islands, and maybe a spark of light from a candle in a cabin window. On the water, we might see a spark or two from a raft or scow, and occasionally we'd hear the sound of a fiddle or a song coming from one of those crafts. Living on a raft was lovely. We'd gaze up at the starry sky and discuss whether the stars were created or just happened to be there. Jim thought they were made, but I believed they just happened. I figured it would take too long to create so many stars. Jim suggested that the moon could have laid them, which seemed somewhat reasonable, so I didn't argue against it. After all, I'd seen a frog lay almost as many eggs, so it was possible. We'd also watch the shooting stars and see them streak across the sky. Jim thought they'd been thrown out of the nest because they'd gone bad. On certain nights, we'd see a steamboat gliding through the darkness, and occasionally it would spew out a cloud of sparks from its chimneys, which would rain down into the river and look beautiful. Then it would turn a corner, its lights would disappear, and the noise would stop, leaving the river quiet once again. Later, its waves would reach us, rocking the raft gently, and after that, we wouldn't hear anything for a long time, except maybe the sound of frogs. After midnight, the people on shore would go to bed, and for a few hours, the shores would be dark, with no more sparks in the cabin windows. Those sparks served as our clock - the first one to reappear would signal that morning was approaching, so we'd quickly find a place to hide and tie up. One morning, just before daybreak, I found a canoe and crossed over a chute to the main shore, which was only about two hundred yards away. I paddled about a mile up a creek surrounded by cypress woods, looking for some berries. As I was passing a spot where a kind of cowpath crossed the creek, I saw two men running up the path as fast as they could. I thought I was in trouble, figuring that whenever someone was chasing someone, it was probably me - or maybe Jim.

Jim thought it was ghosts, but I said, 'No way, ghosts wouldn't say, "Dern the dern fog."' As soon as it got dark, we pushed off and let the current take us wherever it wanted. We'd just float, smoke our pipes, and hang our legs over the side of the raft, talking about all sorts of things. We were always naked, day and night, as long as the mosquitoes didn't bother us too much. The new clothes Buck's family had made for me were too nice to be comfortable, and to be honest, I wasn't really into clothes anyway. Sometimes we'd have the whole river to ourselves for hours. You could see the banks and islands across the water, and occasionally a light from a cabin window or a raft. You might even hear someone playing a fiddle or singing. It was amazing to live on a raft. We'd lie on our backs and stare up at the stars, debating whether they were created or just happened to be there. Jim thought they were made, but I thought they just happened. I figured it would have taken too long to make that many. Jim said the moon could have laid them, which seemed kind of reasonable, so I didn't argue. I mean, I've seen a frog lay a lot of eggs, so it's possible. We'd also watch the shooting stars and see them streak across the sky. Jim thought they were stars that had gone bad and got thrown out of the sky. A few times a night, we'd see a steamboat gliding through the darkness, and sometimes it would shoot out a bunch of sparks from its chimneys. The sparks would rain down into the river and look really cool. Then the boat would turn a corner, its lights would disappear, and everything would be quiet again. After a while, the waves from the boat would reach us and rock the raft a bit. For a long time after that, all you'd hear would be frogs or something. After midnight, the people on shore would go to bed, and the shores would be dark for a few hours. We used the lights from the cabin windows as a kind of clock - when we saw the first light of the morning, we'd find a place to hide the raft right away. One morning, just before sunrise, I found a canoe and paddled across a small channel to the main shore. I went about a mile up a creek into the cypress woods to see if I could find some berries. As I was passing a spot where a path crossed the creek, I saw two men running down the path as fast as they could. I thought I was in trouble, figuring they must be after me or Jim.

Jim thought the strange noise was made by spirits, but I disagreed. 'Spirits wouldn't say, 'Dern the dern fog,'' I said. As soon as it got dark, we pushed our raft into the water. When we reached the middle of the river, we let it float freely, and then we lit our pipes and hung our legs over the side of the raft. We talked about all sorts of things, and we were usually naked because our clothes were uncomfortable and the mosquitoes would bite us if we wore them. We could see the banks and islands on the other side of the water, and occasionally we'd see a light from a cabin window or a raft. We might even hear someone playing a fiddle or singing. It was great to live on a raft. We'd lie on our backs and look up at the stars, wondering if they were made or just happened to be there. Jim thought they were made, but I thought they just happened. I figured it would take too long to make that many stars. Jim said the moon could have laid them, which seemed possible, so I didn't argue. We'd watch the stars that fell from the sky and see them streak down. Jim thought they'd gotten spoiled and were thrown out of the sky. At night, we'd sometimes see a steamboat passing by in the dark. It would shoot out sparks from its chimneys, and they'd fall into the river, looking really pretty. Then the boat would turn a corner, and its lights would disappear. The waves from the boat would reach us after a while, rocking the raft a bit. After that, it would be quiet again, except for the sounds of frogs or other animals. After midnight, the people on shore would go to bed, and the shores would be dark for a few hours. We used the lights from the cabin windows as a kind of clock. When we saw the first light again, we knew morning was coming, so we'd find a place to hide the raft. One morning, I found a canoe and crossed over to the main shore. I paddled up a small stream among the cypress trees, looking for some berries. As I was passing a place where a path crossed the stream, I saw two men running down the path as fast as they could. I thought I was in trouble, thinking that they might be after me or Jim.

It nearly killed Jim with laughter. He was always the easiest person to make laugh. I took the watch, and Jim lay down and started snoring; eventually, the storm subsided completely, and when the first cabin light appeared, I woke him up, and we hid the raft for the day. After breakfast, the king pulled out an old, worn-out deck of cards, and he and the duke played a game of seven-up for a while, betting five cents per game. When they got tired of it, they decided to come up with a new plan. The duke rummaged through his carpet-bag and pulled out a bunch of small, printed bills, which he read aloud. One of the bills announced that the 'celebrated Dr. Armand de Montalban, of Paris' would be giving a lecture on phrenology at a certain location, with admission costing ten cents, and character charts available for twenty-five cents each. The duke claimed to be this person. Another bill introduced him as the 'world-renowned Shakespearian tragedian, Garrick the Younger, of Drury Lane, London.' Other bills listed various names and accomplishments, including finding water and gold with a divining rod and breaking witch spells. The duke then said, 'But the theater is my true passion. Have you ever acted on stage, Your Majesty?' The king replied that he hadn't. The duke told him, 'You will, then, before you're three days older. The first decent town we come across, we'll rent a hall and perform the sword fight from Richard III and the balcony scene from Romeo and Juliet. What do you think?' The king agreed, saying he was willing to do anything that would pay, but he didn't know much about acting and hadn't seen many plays. The duke assured him it would be easy to learn. The king was eager to start, so the duke began explaining the story of Romeo and Juliet, saying he would play Romeo and the king could play Juliet. The king expressed concern that his appearance might not be suitable for the role, given his age and balding head. The duke dismissed his worries, saying that the audience wouldn't notice, and that costumes would make all the difference. He produced a few old curtain-calico suits, which he claimed were medieval armor, and a long white cotton nightshirt and ruffled nightcap for the king to wear as Juliet. The king was satisfied, so the duke read the parts aloud in a dramatic fashion, acting out the scenes to demonstrate how it should be done. Then, he handed the book to the king and told him to memorize his lines. There was a small town about three miles down the river, and after dinner, the duke said he had figured out a way to travel during the day without putting Jim in danger. He decided to go into town to make the necessary arrangements.

It almost killed Jim laughing. He was the easiest person to make laugh that ever was, anyway. I took the watch, and Jim lay down and snored away; and by and by the storm let up for good; and the first cabin light that showed, I woke him up and we slid the raft into hiding for the day. The king got out an old deck of cards after breakfast, and he and the duke played a game called seven-up for a while, five cents a game. Then they got tired of it, and decided they would 'lay out a campaign,' as they called it. The duke went down into his bag, and fetched up a lot of little printed bills and read them out loud. One bill said, 'The celebrated Dr. Armand de Montalban, of Paris,' would 'lecture on the Science of Phrenology' at a certain place, on a certain day, at ten cents admission, and 'furnish charts of character at twenty-five cents apiece.' The duke said that was him. In another bill, he was the 'world-renowned Shakespearian actor, Garrick the Younger, of Drury Lane, London.' In other bills, he had a lot of other names and did other amazing things, like finding water and gold with a 'divining rod,' 'breaking witch spells,' and so on. After a while, he says: 'But acting is my true love. Have you ever been on stage, Royalty?' 'No,' says the king. 'You will, then, before you're three days older, Fallen Grandeur,' says the duke. 'The first good town we come to, we'll hire a hall and perform the sword fight in Richard III and the balcony scene in Romeo and Juliet. How does that sound?' 'I'm in, all the way, for anything that will pay, Bilgewater; but, you see, I don't know much about acting, and haven't seen much of it. I was too small when my dad used to have performances at the palace. Do you think you can teach me?' 'Easy!' 'All right. I'm just looking for something new, anyway. Let's start right away.' So the duke told him all about who Romeo was and who Juliet was, and said he was used to playing Romeo, so the king could be Juliet. 'But if Juliet's such a young girl, duke, my bald head and my white whiskers are going to look pretty odd on her, maybe.' 'Don't worry; these country people won't think twice about that. Besides, you'll be in costume, and that makes all the difference; Juliet's in a balcony, enjoying the moonlight before she goes to bed, and she's wearing her nightgown and her ruffled nightcap.' He got out two or three old-fashioned suits, which he said were medieval armor for Richard III and the other character, and a long white cotton nightshirt and a ruffled nightcap to match. The king was satisfied; so the duke got out his book and read the parts out loud in a very dramatic way, acting at the same time, to show how it had to be done; then he gave the book to the king and told him to memorize his part. There was a small town about three miles down the river, and after dinner, the duke said he had figured out his idea about how to travel in daylight without it being dangerous for Jim; so he said he would go down to the town and take care of that.
